::: {.why}
Regulators moved to expected shortfall for a reason that is a mathematical property rather than a preference, and being able to state it precisely is a question that gets asked.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the subadditivity property, give a two-position example where VaR violates it, and say why expected shortfall does not.
- Report expected shortfall alongside VaR for your book and say which you would use for sizing.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Construct the counterexample rather than reading one: two positions each with a small probability of a large loss, arranged so the combined VaR at 95 percent exceeds the sum of the individual VaRs. Then show expected shortfall is subadditive on the same example.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Compute expected shortfall at 97.5 percent for your book under all three estimators from yesterday, and compare against the 99 percent VaR. Then note which quantity is harder to estimate and why, since expected shortfall depends on the tail shape rather than on a single quantile.
:::
:::
